screens.title: Mobile Inverted Pendulum Simulation
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter teaches you to model and simulate a Mobile Inverted Pendulum, a two-wheeled balancing robot that must keep an upright chassis while moving. You will learn how the nonlinear dynamics come from the Lagrangian equations, why we linearize about the upright position, and how to arrange a two-loop PD controller: a fast inner balance loop and a slower outer position loop. You'll also build an Extended Kalman Filter to fuse noisy IMU and encoder data into a reliable state estimate, and run a MATLAB simulation to observe position and angle responses over time. A concrete example you will implement is simulating the robot from an initial small tilt, tuning gains to achieve stable balance, and commanding a position move at three seconds to see the robot tilt forward then back to stop. Importantly, we will highlight the stability limits: linear controllers work near the upright equilibrium, and large initial tilts can make recovery impossible. By the end you will understand the full pipeline from physics to controller, estimator, and simulation, and you will be ready to implement the MIP capstone in MATLAB.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the hands-on path. First, you will model the Mobile Inverted Pendulum dynamics as a two-wheeled robot and identify the state variables: wheel position and velocity, and pendulum angle and angular velocity. Modeling grounds the controller and estimator design and connects the physics to code. Second, you will design a cascade PD controller: an inner loop that quickly stabilizes angle, and an outer loop that produces a small desired tilt to move the robot to a target position. This split solves different time-scale problems cleanly and makes tuning tractable. Third, you will implement an Extended Kalman Filter to estimate the full four-state vector from noisy IMU and encoder measurements. The EKF prediction uses the linearized dynamics and the update fuses angle, rate, and encoder velocity. Finally, you will simulate the complete system in MATLAB using ode45, examine plots of position and angle, test gain variations, and observe failure modes when the initial tilt is too large. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify your implementation in simulation.

screens.title: Objective Details and Milestones
screens.narratorSegment: Here we expand the milestones with practical verification and a short mnemonic to remember each skill. For modeling, verify your nonlinear equations by checking units and special cases: set pendulum mass to zero and ensure wheel dynamics reduce correctly. That quick check helps catch algebraic errors. For control, remember the nested-loop mnemonic: balance fast, move slow. Verify by first tuning the inner PD until the angle response is stable for small disturbances, then add the outer loop to follow a position command. For EKF estimation, practice by adding Gaussian noise to the IMU and encoder in simulation and compare the filtered estimate to the true state; this shows filter performance and helps tune Q and R. For simulation, run the three gain scenarios provided: too-low balance gain, too-high balance gain, and well-tuned gains so you can see oscillation, high-frequency response, and stable balance. Each verification gives you confidence before transferring code to hardware.

screens.title: What is the Mobile Inverted Pendulum (MIP)?
screens.narratorSegment: The Mobile Inverted Pendulum is a two-wheeled robot with a chassis that behaves like an inverted pendulum. The key idea is that the chassis must be kept upright while the wheels drive the base to control position. The MIP state is four-dimensional: wheel position x and velocity x dot, pendulum angle theta and angular velocity theta dot. These four states are sufficient to describe the robot's translational motion and its rotational balance dynamics in the plane. A concrete example is a Segway-style platform: the IMU measures angle and angular rate while wheel encoders measure wheel motion. One common misconception is to treat wheel velocity alone as sufficient for control; in fact, angle and angular velocity are critical because balance is the fast dynamic that must be stabilized before position can be reliably controlled. For simulation and control, represent the state as a column vector x equals bracket x, x dot, theta, theta dot close bracket so that you can write dynamics compactly and design state-feedback controllers and observers. Consider how sensor choices map to state observability when you plan the EKF update.

keyIdea.title: State vector
keyIdea.text: MIP state is [x; ẋ; θ; θ̇] — wheel position/velocity and pendulum angle/angular velocity.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › What is the MIP?
Definition and physical parts
Two wheels, a chassis that can tilt, motors that apply torque to the wheels, and an IMU plus encoders for sensing.
State variables
  • x: wheel position (m)
  • ẋ: wheel linear velocity (m/s)
  • θ: pendulum (chassis) angle from upright (rad)
  • θ̇: angular velocity (rad/s)
Why this matters

You must estimate and control both position and angle. Angle dynamics are fast and require aggressive feedback; position is a slower outer objective.

Sensors and observability
IMU provides angle and angular rate directly, encoders provide wheel velocity. Together these measurements enable an EKF to estimate the full four-state vector if you design the observation matrix correctly.
Concrete scenario
Start simulation with θ = 0.1 rad. The IMU reads noisy θ and θ̇; the encoder reads ẋ with noise. A well-tuned EKF produces a smooth estimate usable by the PD controllers for balance and position control.

screens.title: Nonlinear Dynamics from Lagrangian Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: The MIP dynamics emerge by applying Lagrangian mechanics to the wheel-pendulum system and result in coupled, nonlinear differential equations. The important nonlinear terms are sin(theta), cos(theta), and terms proportional to theta dot squared, which represent centrifugal effects. In the 2D simplified model the equations are: open parenthesis M plus m close parenthesis times x double dot plus m L theta double dot cos theta minus m L theta dot squared sin theta equals F, and m L x double dot cos theta plus open parenthesis m L squared plus I close parenthesis theta double dot minus m g L sin theta equals minus F L cos theta. These relate the applied wheel force F to the translational acceleration and to the pendulum accelerations, and they show how wheel motion and pendulum motion are coupled. A concrete example to keep in mind: if theta is small, the sin and cos terms are approximated by theta and one, simplifying control design. A common misconception is to drop the theta dot squared term without testing; in maneuvers with nonzero angular speeds, that term produces significant dynamics. When you implement the nonlinear dynamics in code, verify special cases and unit consistency before trusting simulation results.

keyIdea.title: Nonlinear coupling
keyIdea.text: Dynamics include sin(θ), cos(θ), and θ̇² terms that couple wheel and pendulum accelerations; these must be coded correctly for accurate simulation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Nonlinear Dynamics
Lagrangian-derived equations
Coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations that govern MIP behavior.
(M + m) * ẍ + m * L * θ̈ * cos(θ) - m * L * θ̇² * sin(θ) = F
m * L * ẍ * cos(θ) + (m * L² + I) * θ̈ - m * g * L * sin(θ) = -F * L * cos(θ)
Concrete check
Set θ to zero and verify that the equations reduce to coupled wheel dynamics without trigonometric terms. Test numerical behavior for small and moderate θ̇ to ensure θ̇² term is handled stably in simulation.
Implementation notes
  • Compute cos and sin once per step to avoid repeated evaluation.
  • Beware of sign conventions when mapping motor torque to force F.
  • Validate units: mass, length, inertia, gravity must be consistent.
Key takeaway

Nonlinear terms matter for realistic maneuvers; do not drop them without verifying effects in simulation.

screens.title: Linearization Around the Upright Equilibrium
screens.narratorSegment: Designing linear controllers requires a linear model. We linearize the nonlinear MIP equations about the upright equilibrium where theta equals zero and theta dot equals zero. Using small-angle approximations sin(theta) approximates theta and cos(theta) approximates one, the dynamics reduce to two linear equations: open parenthesis M plus m close parenthesis times x double dot plus m L theta double dot equals F, and m L x double dot plus open parenthesis m L squared plus I close parenthesis theta double dot minus m g L theta equals minus F L. From these linear equations you can obtain state-space matrices A and B that express x dot equals A times x plus B times u where x is the four-state vector and u is the applied force F. A common pitfall is assuming linearization is valid for large tilts; it is only valid in a neighborhood around the upright position. In practice you will design controllers with the linear model and then test them in the full nonlinear simulation to confirm they work within the intended operating region. Always check the region of attraction by running simulations from different initial tilts.

keyIdea.text: Linearization yields A and B matrices for controller design, but validity is limited to small angles near the upright equilibrium.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Linearization
Linearize about θ = 0
Replace sin(θ) with θ and cos(θ) with 1 to obtain linear dynamics for controller design.
(M + m) * ẍ + m * L * θ̈ = F
m * L * ẍ + (m * L² + I) * θ̈ - m * g * L * θ = -F * L
From here to A and B
Rearrange these linear equations into first-order form ẋ = A x + B u with x = [x, ẋ, θ, θ̇]. These matrices feed pole-placement or LQR design methods.
Practical note
Test linear-controller designs in the full nonlinear simulator from different initial tilts to estimate the valid operating range and region of attraction.
Common mistake

Tuning solely on the linear model without nonlinear simulation can hide failures for larger tilts; always validate in the nonlinear model.

screens.title: State-Space Representation and Controller Options
screens.narratorSegment: Once the linearized equations are available, write them in state-space form x dot equals A x plus B u with the four-state vector x equals bracket x, ẋ, theta, theta dot close bracket and u equal to the applied wheel force F. The A matrix encodes dynamics coupling between position and angle; B maps the control input into accelerations. With A and B available you have multiple controller design choices: pole placement or LQR for full-state feedback, or simpler cascade PD loops that directly control angle and position in nested loops. For this capstone we use a cascade PD approach because it separates fast balance from slow position, simplifying tuning. A common misconception is that state-feedback always outperforms PD loops; in practice, nested PD is robust and easier when only a few gains are needed and when measurement noise and implementation simplicity matter. When designing any controller, compute closed-loop poles to check stability and run time-domain simulations to inspect transient response. Save the A and B matrices in your MATLAB workspace to support EKF prediction and controller synthesis. State-Space Representation and Controller Options means a and b matrices let you design full-state controllers and serve the ekf prediction step; cascade pd offers practical ease for mip balance and motion.. In practical terms, express the linearized model as ẋ = a x + b u and choose a control design method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › State-Space & Control
Form ẋ = A x + B u
Compute A and B from the linearized equations and use them for controller and EKF prediction steps.
Controller choices
  • Pole placement or LQR using full-state feedback.
  • Nesting two PD loops: inner for θ, outer for position to produce θ_des.
  • Simplicity and robustness often favor cascade PD for practical MIP tasks.
EKF integration
Use A and B for the EKF prediction x_pred = A x + B F and P_pred = A P A' + Q in discrete or continuous-time approximations.
Concrete tip
Store symbolic or numeric A and B in MATLAB and compare eigenvalues of A with closed-loop eigenvalues after applying your feedback gains.

screens.title: Cascade PD Controller — Inner Loop (Balance)
screens.narratorSegment: The inner loop's role is to stabilize the pendulum angle quickly. Its control law is τ_balance equals Kp_theta times open bracket zero minus theta close bracket plus Kd_theta times open bracket zero minus theta dot close bracket. In other words, the controller applies torque proportional to angle error and angular rate error to return theta toward zero. Think of balancing a broom: small angular deviations call for quick corrective motions. A concrete example is choosing Kp_theta of 50 and Kd_theta of 10 in simulation; with these values the angle returns to upright from small tilts with a damped response. A common tuning mistake is choosing Kp too small, which yields slow, growing oscillations, or Kp too large with insufficient derivative action, which produces high-frequency oscillation. When tuning, start with a moderate proportional gain, add derivative to damp oscillation, then validate that the inner loop responds faster than any outer-loop commands. Always test inner-loop robustness with simulated IMU noise and ensure the EKF provides angle and rate estimates fast enough for feedback. Cascade PD Controller — Inner Loop (Balance) means tau_balance = kp_theta*(0 - θ) + kd_theta*(0 - θ̇). tune for fast, damped angle correction before adding outer-loop objectives.. In practical terms, fast pd action to keep the pendulum upright. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inner PD law
keyIdea.text: tau_balance = Kp_theta*(0 - θ) + Kd_theta*(0 - θ̇). Tune for fast, damped angle correction before adding outer-loop objectives.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Inner Loop
Balance controller
A PD controller stabilizes θ around zero with fast, damped corrections.
τ_balance = Kp_theta * (0 - θ) + Kd_theta * (0 - θ̇)
Tuning checklist
  • Start with Kp moderate, add Kd to reduce overshoot.
  • Validate stability from small initial tilts in nonlinear sim.
  • Ensure sampling and estimator latency are low for effective derivative action.
Example gains
Kp_theta = 50, Kd_theta = 10 often produces a fast, damped angle response in simulation for small tilts; test and adjust for your parameters.
Pitfall

Derivative action amplifies sensor noise; use EKF-filtered angular rate rather than raw noisy gyro if possible.

screens.title: Cascade PD Controller — Outer Loop (Position)
screens.narratorSegment: The outer loop controls the robot's position by commanding a small desired tilt angle. The outer PD control law computes x_des equals Kp_x times open bracket x_target minus x close bracket plus Kd_x times open bracket zero minus x dot close bracket. Then you convert this into a desired angle by dividing by the pendulum length L: theta_des equals x_des divided by L. That small theta_des is fed into the inner PD controller which acts to bring theta to theta_des, causing the wheels to accelerate and move the robot. A concrete scenario is commanding x_target of two meters at t equals three seconds; the outer loop produces a small forward tilt, the inner loop stabilizes to that tilt while the robot accelerates, then the outer loop commands a negative tilt to stop at the target. A common misconception is to set theta_des too large; this can push the system out of the linear region and cause the inner loop to fail. Tune outer-loop gains for moderate, slow motion and ensure the inner loop bandwidth is substantially higher than the outer loop.

keyIdea.title: Outer loop mapping
keyIdea.text: x_des = Kp_x*(x_target - x) + Kd_x*(0 - ẋ); θ_des = x_des / L. Outer loop is slower and produces small tilt commands for motion.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Outer Loop
Position controller to tilt mapping
Outer loop computes a target tilt proportional to position error so the inner loop causes motion.
x_des = Kp_x * (x_target - x) + Kd_x * (0 - ẋ)
θ_des = x_des / L
Behavioral example
At t = 3s command x_target = 2 m. Outer loop issues a small θ_des forward, inner loop tracks θ_des, wheels accelerate, and the robot moves toward the target.
Tuning advice
  • Keep outer gains low so θ_des remains small.
  • Ensure inner loop bandwidth is an order of magnitude higher than the outer loop.
  • Simulate step commands to observe smooth acceleration and deceleration.

screens.title: Combined Control Law and Tuning Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Combine the outer-loop desired tilt with the inner PD balance law to obtain the total input F. Practically the inner loop controls θ toward θ_des, and the actuator force F is computed as F equals Kp_theta times open bracket θ_des minus θ close bracket plus Kd_theta times open bracket zero minus θ̇ close bracket. This composition means the inner loop sees a reference that is generated by position error. When tuning, balance responsiveness and robustness: too low Kp_theta yields slow recovery; too high Kp_theta with small Kd_theta gives underdamped high-amplitude oscillations. For outer-loop gains, high Kp_x makes the robot aggressively tilt for position correction, which risks leaving the small-angle region. A typical exercise is to run three tests: too-low Kp_theta to observe unstable oscillation, too-high Kp_theta to observe high-frequency jitter, and well-chosen gains for stable balance. A useful contrast is to compare cascade PD to a single full-state LQR: LQR can provide optimal trade-offs but requires full-state feedback and a model; cascade PD is simpler to implement and tune, especially when using EKF estimates rather than full state measurement. Combined Control Law and Tuning Considerations means f = kp_theta*(θ_des - θ) + kd_theta*(0 - θ̇). tune inner loop for fast damping and outer loop for gentle motion to avoid leaving linear region.. Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Combined Control
Total control input
Inner loop tracks θ_des produced by the outer loop; the total force sent to wheels is from the inner PD.
F = Kp_theta * (θ_des - θ) + Kd_theta * (0 - θ̇)
where θ_des = (Kp_x * (x_target - x) + Kd_x * (0 - ẋ)) / L
Tuning scenarios

  • Too-high Kp_theta: high-frequency oscillation; rely on Kd to damp.
  • Good gains: stable balance and smooth position changes when commanded.
Practical comparison
Cascade PD is easier to tune in practice; full-state LQR is model-dependent but can be optimal. Use cascade PD for the capstone to emphasize robustness and simplicity.

screens.title: EKF for State Estimation
screens.narratorSegment: State estimation is essential because sensors provide noisy, partial observations. We implement an Extended Kalman Filter that predicts the next state using the linearized dynamics and then updates the state using IMU and encoder measurements. The measurement vector z contains theta_imu, theta_dot_imu, and x_dot_encoder. In prediction: x_pred equals A times x plus B times F and P_pred equals A P A transpose plus Q. In the update step compute H, the observation matrix reflecting which states map to measurements: rows for theta, theta_dot, and x_dot. Compute the Kalman gain K equals P_pred H transpose times inverse of H P_pred H transpose plus R. Then update x equals x_pred plus K times z minus H x_pred and update covariance P accordingly. A common confusion is treating the EKF as a low-pass filter; instead it optimally balances model uncertainty and measurement noise when Q and R are tuned. In practice, initialize P to a reasonable uncertainty, choose Q for process noise, and set R to sensor noise covariance. Verify the filter by injecting Gaussian noise into sensors and comparing estimated state to the simulated truth.

keyIdea.text: Predict with A and B, compute P_pred, compute K with H and R, update x and P. Tune Q and R to balance model and sensor uncertainty.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › EKF
EKF prediction and update
Use the linearized A and B for the prediction; update with IMU and encoder observations.
% EKF prediction
x_pred = A * x + B * F;
P_pred = A * P * A' + Q;

% EKF update
H = [0 0 1 0; 0 0 0 1; 0 1 0 0];
K = P_pred * H' / (H * P_pred * H' + R);
x = x_pred + K * (z - H * x_pred);
P = (eye(4) - K * H) * P_pred;
Concrete test

Add Gaussian noise to IMU and encoder in simulation and verify the EKF estimate closely tracks the true state while smoothing high-frequency noise.

Practical tips
  • Initialize P with large values if initial state is uncertain.
  • Tune Q to represent model and unmodeled disturbances.
  • Set R from sensor calibration or measured noise variance.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › MATLAB Simulation
Simulation skeleton
Define parameters, gains, implement dynamics function, run ode45, and plot position and angle.
% Parameters
M = 0.5; m = 1.0; L = 0.3; I = 0.1; g = 9.81;
Kp_theta = 50; Kd_theta = 10; Kp_x = 2; Kd_x = 1;

% Simulate
tspan = [0 10];
x0 = [0; 0; 0.1; 0];
[t, x] = ode45(@(t,x) mip_dynamics(t, x, Kp_theta, Kd_theta, Kp_x, Kd_x, M, m, L, I, g), tspan, x0);

% Plot
figure;
subplot(2,1,1); plot(t, x(:,1)); ylabel('Position (m)');
subplot(2,1,2); plot(t, x(:,3)); ylabel('Pendulum Angle (rad)'); xlabel('Time (s)');
Add simulated sensor noise for IMU and encoders, run the EKF in parallel, and overlay estimated states on the plots to assess filter performance.
Simulation experiments
  • Test three gain scenarios: too low, too high, and good.
  • At t = 3s set x_target = 2 m and observe tilt-based acceleration.

screens.title: Stability Limits and Fail-Safe Mechanisms
screens.narratorSegment: The MIP is naturally unstable. Linear controllers designed around the upright equilibrium work only within a finite region of attraction. In simulation, a common threshold is roughly plus or minus thirty degrees; outside this range the linearized model and PD gains may not provide enough torque to recover and the robot will fall. A concrete safety practice for physical systems is to implement a fall detector that measures absolute angle and disables motors when the tilt exceeds a safe threshold, preventing damage. In simulation you can still observe failure modes to understand how the controller behaves near the edge of stability: large initial tilts may cause the controller to saturate actuators or produce excessive oscillation. A misconception to avoid is treating simulation success with small initial tilts as evidence of robustness; always test multiple initial conditions and noisy sensors. For hardware, add fail-safe power cutoff and mechanical bumpers; in simulation, log actuator saturation and state trajectories to learn safe operating envelopes. Stability Limits and Fail-Safe Mechanisms means linear controllers have a limited region of stability; detect large tilt and cut power on hardware to prevent damage.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Safety & Failure Modes
Stability limits
Linear controllers are valid only near the upright equilibrium; test limits in simulation and enforce hardware cutoffs.
Failure example
Initial θ = 1 rad (~57°) is outside the linear region; the linearized controller can fail to recover and the robot will fall in simulation.
Hardware fail-safes
Monitor absolute angle and cut motor power if tilt exceeds a safe threshold. Log actuation saturation and avoid aggressive outer-loop commands that request large θ_des.
Simulation checks
  • Run multiple initial tilts to find region of attraction.
  • Record when actuators saturate and note resulting motion.
  • Compare linear-controller predictions with nonlinear outcomes.

fullNarratorScript:
This chapter teaches you to model and simulate a Mobile Inverted Pendulum, a two-wheeled balancing robot that must keep an upright chassis while moving. You will learn how the nonlinear dynamics come from the Lagrangian equations, why we linearize about the upright position, and how to arrange a two-loop PD controller: a fast inner balance loop and a slower outer position loop. You'll also build an Extended Kalman Filter to fuse noisy IMU and encoder data into a reliable state estimate, and run a MATLAB simulation to observe position and angle responses over time. A concrete example you will implement is simulating the robot from an initial small tilt, tuning gains to achieve stable balance, and commanding a position move at three seconds to see the robot tilt forward then back to stop. Importantly, we will highlight the stability limits: linear controllers work near the upright equilibrium, and large initial tilts can make recovery impossible. By the end you will understand the full pipeline from physics to controller, estimator, and simulation, and you will be ready to implement the MIP capstone in MATLAB.

These objectives guide the hands-on path. First, you will model the Mobile Inverted Pendulum dynamics as a two-wheeled robot and identify the state variables: wheel position and velocity, and pendulum angle and angular velocity. Modeling grounds the controller and estimator design and connects the physics to code. Second, you will design a cascade PD controller: an inner loop that quickly stabilizes angle, and an outer loop that produces a small desired tilt to move the robot to a target position. This split solves different time-scale problems cleanly and makes tuning tractable. Third, you will implement an Extended Kalman Filter to estimate the full four-state vector from noisy IMU and encoder measurements. The EKF prediction uses the linearized dynamics and the update fuses angle, rate, and encoder velocity. Finally, you will simulate the complete system in MATLAB using ode45, examine plots of position and angle, test gain variations, and observe failure modes when the initial tilt is too large. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify your implementation in simulation.

Here we expand the milestones with practical verification and a short mnemonic to remember each skill. For modeling, verify your nonlinear equations by checking units and special cases: set pendulum mass to zero and ensure wheel dynamics reduce correctly. That quick check helps catch algebraic errors. For control, remember the nested-loop mnemonic: balance fast, move slow. Verify by first tuning the inner PD until the angle response is stable for small disturbances, then add the outer loop to follow a position command. For EKF estimation, practice by adding Gaussian noise to the IMU and encoder in simulation and compare the filtered estimate to the true state; this shows filter performance and helps tune Q and R. For simulation, run the three gain scenarios provided: too-low balance gain, too-high balance gain, and well-tuned gains so you can see oscillation, high-frequency response, and stable balance. Each verification gives you confidence before transferring code to hardware.

The Mobile Inverted Pendulum is a two-wheeled robot with a chassis that behaves like an inverted pendulum. The key idea is that the chassis must be kept upright while the wheels drive the base to control position. The MIP state is four-dimensional: wheel position x and velocity x dot, pendulum angle theta and angular velocity theta dot. These four states are sufficient to describe the robot's translational motion and its rotational balance dynamics in the plane. A concrete example is a Segway-style platform: the IMU measures angle and angular rate while wheel encoders measure wheel motion. One common misconception is to treat wheel velocity alone as sufficient for control; in fact, angle and angular velocity are critical because balance is the fast dynamic that must be stabilized before position can be reliably controlled. For simulation and control, represent the state as a column vector x equals bracket x, x dot, theta, theta dot close bracket so that you can write dynamics compactly and design state-feedback controllers and observers. Consider how sensor choices map to state observability when you plan the EKF update.

The MIP dynamics emerge by applying Lagrangian mechanics to the wheel-pendulum system and result in coupled, nonlinear differential equations. The important nonlinear terms are sin(theta), cos(theta), and terms proportional to theta dot squared, which represent centrifugal effects. In the 2D simplified model the equations are: open parenthesis M plus m close parenthesis times x double dot plus m L theta double dot cos theta minus m L theta dot squared sin theta equals F, and m L x double dot cos theta plus open parenthesis m L squared plus I close parenthesis theta double dot minus m g L sin theta equals minus F L cos theta. These relate the applied wheel force F to the translational acceleration and to the pendulum accelerations, and they show how wheel motion and pendulum motion are coupled. A concrete example to keep in mind: if theta is small, the sin and cos terms are approximated by theta and one, simplifying control design. A common misconception is to drop the theta dot squared term without testing; in maneuvers with nonzero angular speeds, that term produces significant dynamics. When you implement the nonlinear dynamics in code, verify special cases and unit consistency before trusting simulation results.

Designing linear controllers requires a linear model. We linearize the nonlinear MIP equations about the upright equilibrium where theta equals zero and theta dot equals zero. Using small-angle approximations sin(theta) approximates theta and cos(theta) approximates one, the dynamics reduce to two linear equations: open parenthesis M plus m close parenthesis times x double dot plus m L theta double dot equals F, and m L x double dot plus open parenthesis m L squared plus I close parenthesis theta double dot minus m g L theta equals minus F L. From these linear equations you can obtain state-space matrices A and B that express x dot equals A times x plus B times u where x is the four-state vector and u is the applied force F. A common pitfall is assuming linearization is valid for large tilts; it is only valid in a neighborhood around the upright position. In practice you will design controllers with the linear model and then test them in the full nonlinear simulation to confirm they work within the intended operating region. Always check the region of attraction by running simulations from different initial tilts.

Once the linearized equations are available, write them in state-space form x dot equals A x plus B u with the four-state vector x equals bracket x, ẋ, theta, theta dot close bracket and u equal to the applied wheel force F. The A matrix encodes dynamics coupling between position and angle; B maps the control input into accelerations. With A and B available you have multiple controller design choices: pole placement or LQR for full-state feedback, or simpler cascade PD loops that directly control angle and position in nested loops. For this capstone we use a cascade PD approach because it separates fast balance from slow position, simplifying tuning. A common misconception is that state-feedback always outperforms PD loops; in practice, nested PD is robust and easier when only a few gains are needed and when measurement noise and implementation simplicity matter. When designing any controller, compute closed-loop poles to check stability and run time-domain simulations to inspect transient response. Save the A and B matrices in your MATLAB workspace to support EKF prediction and controller synthesis. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The inner loop's role is to stabilize the pendulum angle quickly. Its control law is τ_balance equals Kp_theta times open bracket zero minus theta close bracket plus Kd_theta times open bracket zero minus theta dot close bracket. In other words, the controller applies torque proportional to angle error and angular rate error to return theta toward zero. Think of balancing a broom: small angular deviations call for quick corrective motions. A concrete example is choosing Kp_theta of 50 and Kd_theta of 10 in simulation; with these values the angle returns to upright from small tilts with a damped response. A common tuning mistake is choosing Kp too small, which yields slow, growing oscillations, or Kp too large with insufficient derivative action, which produces high-frequency oscillation. When tuning, start with a moderate proportional gain, add derivative to damp oscillation, then validate that the inner loop responds faster than any outer-loop commands. A concrete scenario is commanding x_target of two meters at t equals three seconds; the outer loop produces a small forward tilt, the inner loop stabilizes to that tilt while the robot accelerates, then the outer loop commands a negative tilt to stop at the target.
